name: Internal Line-of-Business Application
description: A pattern for internal applications used by civil servants and departmental staff to manage business processes, case work, or operational activities. These services typically sit behind corporate identity providers and do not face the public internet directly.
whenToUse: Internal tools used exclusively by authenticated departmental staff
Case management or workflow systems for civil servants
Back-office applications supporting operational business processes
Services where the user base is known, bounded, and authenticated via corporate identity
Applications requiring integration with internal systems and shared services
whenNotToUse: Citizen-facing services that must meet the GOV.UK Service Standard
Services requiring public internet access without VPN or corporate network
High-traffic services with unpredictable scaling requirements
Services handling data above OFFICIAL-SENSITIVE classification
Simple reporting dashboards that could use existing BI tooling

typicalComponents.name: Web Application
typicalComponents.purpose: Provide the user interface for internal business processes and workflows
typicalComponents.technology: React, Angular, or Blazor with internal design system

typicalComponents.name: API Layer
typicalComponents.purpose: Expose business logic as RESTful services for the frontend and integrations

typicalComponents.name: Relational Database
typicalComponents.purpose: Store structured business data, case records, and workflow state

typicalComponents.name: Identity Provider
typicalComponents.purpose: Authenticate users via corporate SSO and enforce role-based access
typicalComponents.technology: Azure AD, Okta, or on-premises Active Directory

typicalComponents.name: Document Store
typicalComponents.purpose: Store and retrieve documents associated with cases or business processes
typicalComponents.technology: SharePoint, S3, or Azure Blob Storage

securityControls: Enforce authentication via corporate identity provider with MFA
Implement role-based access control aligned to business roles and data sensitivity
Restrict network access to corporate network or VPN-connected users
Encrypt data at rest and in transit with organisation-managed keys
Implement audit logging for all data access, modifications, and administrative actions
Apply principle of least privilege for service accounts and API access
resilienceConsiderations: Availability requirements typically lower than citizen-facing (99.5% vs 99.9%)
Maintenance windows acceptable during non-business hours
Single-region deployment often sufficient for internal services
Implement database backups with point-in-time recovery
Design for graceful degradation when upstream internal services are unavailable
costConsiderations: Predictable user base allows right-sizing of compute resources
Licensing costs for commercial software (e.g., SQL Server, SharePoint) may apply
Lower availability requirements reduce infrastructure redundancy costs
Consider existing enterprise agreements for platform services
Factor in corporate identity provider licensing if not already provisioned
operationalConsiderations: Align release cycles with departmental change management processes
User support through internal service desk rather than public channels
Training and onboarding for new staff users
Integration with corporate monitoring and alerting platforms
Compliance with departmental architecture principles and technology standards
questionsToAsk: How many internal users will access the system and what are their roles?
Is the corporate identity provider already provisioned or does it need setup?
What existing internal systems does this need to integrate with?
Are there departmental technology standards that constrain technology choices?
What is the acceptable maintenance window for planned downtime?
Is there an existing internal design system or component library to follow?
commonMistakes: Over-engineering availability for an internal service that only operates during business hours
Not integrating with the corporate identity provider, creating a separate credential silo
Building custom document management when SharePoint or existing platforms would suffice
Ignoring departmental architecture principles and creating shadow IT
Not planning for data migration from legacy systems being replaced
